title: Mara and the Interior
premise: Orsen Zhou, once the conservatory's most celebrated piano prodigy, returns five years after a public breakdown to work as its janitor, hiding in plain sight among the people who remember their hands. When a stranger at their mother's funeral addresses the family by a name no one uses—a name from a life Orsen's mother fled—Orsen is forced to confront the sentence their mother never finished translating, written on the back of a deed to the house now slated for sale. As Orsen pieces together the mother's hidden history with help from a disgruntled archivist and a teenage niece who refuses to let them disappear again, they discover that invisibility was always a choice made for them, not by them. The novel ends with Orsen playing publicly for the first time since the breakdown, reading the translated sentence aloud at the house's final open house, and choosing to be known—even though the house, and the old life it protected, is gone.
about_author: Mara Blackwood is the pen name of a former conservatory custodian who spent six years writing during night shifts and claims the mop closet had better acoustics than any practice room. Their work explores the quiet violence of reinvention and the families we assemble when the given ones fail.

chapters.title: The Acoustics of Empty Rooms
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Five years after walking off stage mid-concerto, Orsen mops the conservatory floors at dawn, memorizing which practice rooms hold music worth overhearing. The funeral notice for their mother arrives folded inside a utility bill. Emotional beat: the numb competence of someone who has mistaken avoidance for peace.

chapters.title: A Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. At the sparsely attended funeral, a stranger in an ill-fitting coat calls the family 'the Wei household'—a surname that appears nowhere on any document Orsen has ever seen. The stranger leaves before Orsen can follow. Emotional beat: the floor tilting; grief interrupted by a question with teeth.

chapters.title: Inventory
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV, shifting to the niece Junie's diary entries between sections. Sorting the house for sale, Orsen finds the deed annotated in their mother's hand with half a sentence in Mandarin, unfinished: 'What I could not say was—'. Emotional beat: the discovery that silence was architecture, built deliberately.

chapters.title: The Archivist Who Hates Music
chapters.summary: Third person limited on Wren Okafor, a conservatory archivist who catalogued Orsen's rise and fall and resents being asked to help. Wren agrees anyway, trading access to sealed student files for Orsen's honest account of the breakdown. Emotional beat: two keepers of secrets negotiating terms.

chapters.title: Wei
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. The records reveal the mother performed under the name Lin Wei before defecting, erasing a career—and possibly a family—left behind. The stranger reappears at the conservatory, asking Orsen if they are 'the daughter who doesn't play.' Emotional beat: identity as inheritance and as theft.

chapters.title: Junie Refuses to Be Quiet
chapters.summary: Junie's POV. Sixteen and furious, Junie confronts Orsen about years of absence, demanding to know why the family keeps shrinking itself. She found the stranger's card in her grandmother's coat pocket. Emotional beat: found family asserted loudly against the gravity of shame.

chapters.title: The Sentence, Half-Translated
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. With Wren and Junie, Orsen translates most of the mother's sentence—it concerns a brother left behind and a promise made at a border—but the final clause resists translation, its grammar broken deliberately. The house sale deadline moves up. Emotional beat: the terror of almost understanding.

chapters.title: What the Hands Remember
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren uncovers a recording of the mother performing under the name Wei—playing the same concerto Orsen abandoned. Listening together, Orsen's hands begin moving on the janitor's cart handle. Emotional beat: grief transposed into muscle memory; the body voting before the mind consents.

chapters.title: The Open House
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. At the house's final showing, the stranger arrives—the mother's brother's son, carrying the other half of the letter. Orsen sits at the neglected upright piano and plays the concerto through, then reads the completed sentence aloud: what she could not say was that leaving was the only way she knew to love them. Emotional beat: climax; visibility chosen at last, at cost.

chapters.title: After the Sale Closes
chapters.summary: Junie's POV, closing with Orsen's final entry. The house sells; the family scatters into something new rather than smaller. Orsen accepts a position teaching adult beginners at the conservatory, and Junie moves into Wren's spare room for the school year. Emotional beat: resolution—not restoration, but a family rebuilt on truth instead of silence.
